Notes: c. 33 CE (Paul's conversion; usually dated 31-36 CE, Hengel dates it to 33). Acts 9:1-2, 19-23: Saul asked the high priest 'for letters to the synagogues at Damascus', then 'began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues' and 'confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus'; 'the Jews plotted to kill him'. Earliest documented Jewish residents in the period: an organized community with more than one synagogue, i.e. a sizeable community; no count. Year Established basis: this attestation. Not used: 1 Kings 20:34 (Ben-hadad lets Ahab set up 'bazaars' in Damascus, c. 855 BCE), read by the Jewish Encyclopedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica as a quarter for Israelite merchants, because it is a treaty clause in a narrative of debated historicity, not an attestation of residents.

c. 33 CE. Acts 22:12: Paul's baptizer Ananias of Damascus was 'a devout man according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there' - a named Jewish individual and an attestation of a resident Jewish community. No count.

c. 33 CE (Hengel's date for Paul's conversion). Craig L. Blomberg, review of M. Hengel and A. M. Schwemer, Paul between Damascus and Antioch (1997): the authors argue that 'a strong Jewish community in Damascus and an already existing group of God-fearers' make Saul's mission there and his preaching in the synagogues historically credible. Scholarly assessment of a strong community plus gentile sympathizers; no count.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906; R. Gottheil, F. Buhl, M. Franco), 'Damascus': 'At this time about 10,000 Jews lived at Damascus, governed by an ethnarch (Acts ix. 2; II Cor. xi. 32).' 'At this time' refers to Paul's activity, which the article dates to 49 CE (year used as given). Estimate of resident Jews by an older reference work; no method stated, and the round figure probably derives from Josephus' massacre figure (War 2.561, 10,000 in Whiston). The reading of the ethnarch of Aretas (2 Cor 11:32) as a Jewish ethnarch is contested (others see him as the Nabataean king's governor or head of the Nabataean colony).

1st c. CE (midpoint 50). Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception vol. 6 (De Gruyter 2013), 'Damascus': R. Riesner (NT section): 'Damascus had a strong Jewish community, including a great number of proselytes (J.W. 2.561; 7.368)'; A. J. Avery-Peck (Judaism section): 'By the first centuries CE, a large Jewish community lived in Damascus, which accounts for Paul's activity there'; A. M. Maeir: 'A large Jewish community existed in Damascus, many of whom were killed during the First Revolt'. Scholarly confirmation of a large community; no number. (Riesner also holds that the 'land of Damascus' of the Damascus Document, CD VII, was a real Essene area of exile in the region; this is contested and not used as evidence of Jews in the city.)

Event, 66 CE, after Cestius Gallus' defeat: Josephus, War 2.20.2 (2.559-561), Greek text (Niese): the Damascenes, having shut the Jews up in the gymnasium ('place of public exercises'), slaughtered 'μυρίους καὶ πεντακοσίους' (10,500; Whiston's translation gives 'ten thousand'), all unarmed, within one hour. They hid the plan from their own wives, who 'all but a few' had been drawn to the Jewish religion (gentile sympathizers/proselytes). Ancient death toll, not a census of residents: Population left blank. It implies a very large resident community but is probably inflated; Josephus does not say that no Jews remained. Life 27 mentions the same calamity.

Event, 66 CE: Josephus, War 7.8.7 (7.368, Eleazar's speech at Masada, Whiston translation): the Damascenes 'cut the throats of eighteen thousand Jews, with their wives and children'. Ancient death-toll figure, which conflicts with the 10,500 of War 2.561; rhetorical and probably exaggerated. Population left blank.
